questions.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Using a Tangent Line Approximation
questions.problem: The graph of the function $f(x)$ passes through $(3,-1)$ and ${f}^{′}(3)=2.$ Find $L(x)$, the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the graph of $f(x)$ passes through $(3,-1)$, we have that $f(3)=-1.$ Therefore, the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $a=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3) \\  & =-1+2(x-3) \\  & =-1+2x-6 \\  & =2x-7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The graph of the function $f(x)$ passes through $(3,6)$ and ${f}^{′}(3)=-5.$ Find $L(x),$ the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the graph of $f(x)$ passes through $(3,6)$, we have that $f(3)=6.$ Therefore, the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $a=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3) \\  & =6-5(x-3) \\  & =6-5x+15 \\  & =-5x+21.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Using a Tangent Line Approximation
questions.problem: Suppose that $f(4.9)=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${f}^{′}(4.9)=5.$ Using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=4.9$, estimate the value of $f(5).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=4.9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(4.9)+{f}^{′}(4.9)(x-4.9) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+5(x-4.9).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(5)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=5.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & ≈L(5) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+5(5-4.9) \\  & =0.5+5(0.1) \\  & =0.5+0.5 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Using a Tangent Line Approximation
questions.problem:
A logistics manager tracks the total distance $s$, in kilometers, traveled by a delivery drone. The following table shows the drone’s speed.

| **$t\,\text{(minutes)}$** | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ | $20$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${s}^{′}(t)\,\text{(km/min)}$ | $0.42$ | $0.48$ | $0.53$ | $0.58$ |

At $t=10,$ the drone had traveled $4.6$ kilometers. Use the tangent line approximation of $s$ at time $t=10$ to estimate the distance traveled at $t=11.$  Do not round the answer.

The distance traveled by the drone at $t=11$ minutes is estimated to be
{{field-1}}
kilometers.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $s(t)$ at the point $a=10$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =s(a)+{s}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =s(10)+{s}^{′}(10)(t-10) \\  & =4.6+0.48(t-10).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $s(11)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=11.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(11) & ≈L(11) \\  & =4.6+0.48(11-10) \\  & =4.6+0.48(1) \\  & =4.6+0.48 \\  & =5.08.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance traveled by the drone at $t=11$ minutes is estimated to be $5.08$ kilometers.

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$ and $f(9)=-10.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=9$ to estimate the value of $f(8.7).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(9)+{f}^{′}(9)(x-9).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(9)=-10,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}},$ then ${f}^{′}(9)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{9}}=-\frac{2}{3}.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-10-\frac{2}{3}(x-9).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(8.7)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=8.7.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(8.7) & ≈L(8.7) \\  & =-10-\frac{2}{3}(8.7-9) \\  & =-10-\frac{2}{3}(-0.3) \\  & =-10+0.2 \\  & =-9.8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $f(\frac{\pi }{4})=0.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ to estimate the value of $f(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(\frac{\pi }{4})=0,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=2(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & ≈L(1) \\  & =2(1-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{3x-4}$ and $f(2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ to estimate the value of $f(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{3x-4},$ then ${f}^{′}(2)=\frac{3}{3(2)-4}=\frac{3}{2}.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}(x-2).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3) & ≈L(3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}(3-2) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6$ and $f(1)=-2.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6,$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=12(1)^{2}-6=6.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2+6(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ≈L(2) \\  & =-2+6(2-1) \\  & =-2+6(1) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=(5x-3)^{2}(4x-2)^{4}$ and $f(0)=3.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ to estimate the value of $f(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(0)=3,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=(5x-3)^{2}(4x-2)^{4},$ then ${f}^{′}(0)=(5(0)-3)^{2}(4(0)-2)^{4}=144.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=3+144x.
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ≈L(2) \\  & =3+144(2) \\  & =3+288 \\  & =291.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent Line Approximation and Classifying it as an Underestimate or Overestimate
questions.problem: Given that the tangent line approximation to the function $f(x)$ at $x=-3$ underestimates the values of the function in the neighborhood of $x=-3,$ which of the following must be true?
questions.worked_solution:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-3$ underestimates the values of the function, we have

$$
L(x)<f(x),
$$

that is, the line $L(x)$ must be below the graph of $f(x)$ near the point  $x=-3.$

Therefore, the function must be concave up in the neighborhood of $x=-3.$

choices.value: $f(x)$ is concave up in the neighborhood of $x=-3$
$f(x)$ is concave down in the neighborhood of $x=-3$

answer_fields.correct_value: $f(x)$ is concave up in the neighborhood of $x=-3$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking confirms the earlier uncertainty: lying above one tangent does not imply concavity throughout a neighborhood. For h=x+3, f(x)=h+h^4(2+sin(1/h)), extended by f(-3)=0, lies strictly above its tangent h nearby, but its concavity oscillates. Its nonzero slope also excludes a local minimum or maximum at -3. Thus none of the choices is guaranteed; option a requires an additional assumption about local concavity.

answers.correct_value: None of the listed statements is guaranteed.

submitted_fields.submitted_value: $f(x)$ is concave up in the neighborhood of $x=-3$

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(1,2)$ and is concave up on the interval $(0,2).$ If ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ estimate the value of $f(0.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(1,2),$ so we have $f(1)=2.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =2+(-2)(x-1) \\  & =2-2(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(0.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=0.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.8) & ≈L(0.8) \\  & =2-2(0.8-1) \\  & =2-2(-0.2) \\  & =2.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(0,2),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph close to $x=1,$ and therefore we have an underestimate.

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(3,5),$ so we have $f(3)=5.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(3)=2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =5+2(x-3) \\  & =5+2x-6 \\  & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.6) & ≈L(2.6) \\  & =2(2.6)-1 \\  & =4.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(2,5),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=3,$ and therefore we have an $\text{overestimate}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Using a Tangent Line Approximation
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that $f(-2) = 0$ and $f'(-2)=2.$ Estimate the value of $f(-1.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =0+2(x+2) \\  & =2(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-1.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-1.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.8) & ≈L(-1.8) \\  & =2(-1.8+2) \\  & =2(0.2) \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Given its Derivative
canonical_examples.problem: Let $g$ be a function such that $g'(x) =\sqrt{x}$ and $g(4) = 3.$ Using the tangent line approximation of $g(x)$ at $x=4,$ estimate the value of $g(3.6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $g(x)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =g(a)+{g}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =g(4)+{g}^{′}(4)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $g(4)=3,$ and since $g'(x)=\sqrt{x},$ then $g'(4)=\sqrt{4}=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =3+2(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $g(3.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(3.6) & ≈L(3.6) \\  & =3+2(3.6-4) \\  & =3+2(-0.4) \\  & =3-0.8 \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent Line Approximation and Classifying it as an Underestimate or Overestimate
canonical_examples.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(-2,-5)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0).$ If $f'(-2)=3$, estimate the value of $f(-2.3)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(-2,-5),$ so we have $f(-2)=-5.$ Also, we're told that $f'(-2)=3,$ so we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-5+3(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-2.3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-2.3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2.3) & ≈L(-2.3) \\  & =-5+3(-2.3+2) \\  & =-5+3(-0.3) \\  & =-5-0.9 \\  & =-5.9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0)$, the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=-2,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.
